name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q01 - Standard electromotive force calculation for Daniell cell

questiontext.text:
Given the standard reduction potentials for the half-cells at \(298\text{ K}\):

\[E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}\]

\[E^\circ_{\text{Zn}^{2+}/\text{Zn}} = -0.76\text{ V}\]

What is the standard cell potential (\(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\)) of the Daniell cell represented as \(\text{Zn(s)} \mid \text{Zn}^{2+}(\text{aq}) \parallel \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq)} \mid \text{Cu(s)}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Standard reduction potential of cathode (right electrode, copper): \(E^\circ_{\text{right}} = +0.34\text{ V}\).
Standard reduction potential of anode (left electrode, zinc): \(E^\circ_{\text{left}} = -0.76\text{ V}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
By IUPAC convention, standard cell potential is computed as the standard reduction potential of the cathode minus the standard reduction potential of the anode.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{right}} - E^\circ_{\text{left}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.34\text{ V} - (-0.76\text{ V}) = 0.34\text{ V} + 0.76\text{ V} = +1.10\text{ V}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The cell potential is positive, corresponding to a spontaneous reaction under standard conditions with a value of \(+1.10\text{ V}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(+1.10\text{ V}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q02 - Conductivity cell constant determination using potassium chloride

questiontext.text: The resistance of a conductivity cell containing \(0.001\text{ M KCl}\) solution at \(298\text{ K}\) is \(1500\ \Omega\). If the conductivity of \(0.001\text{ M KCl}\) solution at \(298\text{ K}\) is \(0.146 \times 10^{-3}\text{ S cm}^{-1}\), what is the cell constant of the conductivity cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Resistance of the cell: \(R = 1500\ \Omega\).
Conductivity of the solution: \(\kappa = 0.146 \times 10^{-3}\text{ S cm}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The cell constant \(G^*\) depends strictly on the geometry of the electrodes (\(l/A\)) and is related directly to resistance and conductivity.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[G^* = \frac{l}{A} = R \times \kappa\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[G^* = 1500\ \Omega \times 0.146 \times 10^{-3}\text{ S cm}^{-1} = 0.219\text{ cm}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The product has units of \(\Omega \times \Omega^{-1}\text{ cm}^{-1} = \text{cm}^{-1}\), yielding \(0.219\text{ cm}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(0.219\text{ cm}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q03 - Molar conductivity calculation of potassium chloride electrolyte

questiontext.text: The conductivity of a \(0.20\text{ M}\) solution of \(\text{KCl}\) at \(298\text{ K}\) is \(0.0248\text{ S cm}^{-1}\). What is its molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_m\)) in \(\text{S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Molar concentration: \(c = 0.20\text{ M} = 0.20\text{ mol L}^{-1}\).
Conductivity: \(\kappa = 0.0248\text{ S cm}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
Convert concentration from \(\text{mol L}^{-1}\) to \(\text{mol cm}^{-3}\) using \(1\text{ L} = 1000\text{ cm}^3\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[\Lambda_m = \frac{\kappa \times 1000}{c}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\Lambda_m = \frac{0.0248\text{ S cm}^{-1} \times 1000\text{ cm}^3\text{ L}^{-1}}{0.20\text{ mol L}^{-1}} = \frac{24.8}{0.20} = 124\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The molar conductivity evaluates to \(124\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(124\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q04 - Electrical charge required for aluminium ion reduction

questiontext.text: How much electrical charge in coulombs is required for the complete electrochemical reduction of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{Al}^{3+}\) ions to metallic aluminium? (Take \(F = 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Amount of substance: \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{Al}^{3+}\).
Faraday constant: \(F = 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Electrode Reaction and Stoichiometry
The reduction half-reaction at the cathode is: \[\text{Al}^{3+} + 3\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Al(s)}\] Reduction of \(1\text{ mol}\) of trivalent aluminium ions requires \(3\text{ moles}\) of electrons (\(3\text{ F}\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[Q = n \times F\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[Q = 3 \times 96487\text{ C} = 289461\text{ C} \approx 2.89 \times 10^5\text{ C}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Three moles of electrons correspond to approximately \(2.89 \times 10^5\text{ C}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(289461\text{ C}\) (or \(2.89 \times 10^5\text{ C}\))

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q05 - Cell electromotive force computation under nonstandard concentration conditions

questiontext.text: A Daniell cell operates at \(298\text{ K}\) with \([\text{Zn}^{2+}] = 0.1\text{ M}\) and \([\text{Cu}^{2+}] = 1.0\text{ M}\). Given that \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 1.10\text{ V}\) and \(\frac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}\), what is the electromotive force (\(E_{\text{cell}}\)) of the cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Standard cell potential: \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 1.10\text{ V}\).
Concentrations: \([\text{Zn}^{2+}] = 0.1\text{ M}\), \([\text{Cu}^{2+}] = 1.0\text{ M}\).
Electrons transferred: \(n = 2\).
Constant factor: \(0.059\text{ V}\) at \(298\text{ K}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
Apply the Nernst equation for the Daniell cell reaction: \[\text{Zn(s)} + \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(\text{aq)} + \text{Cu(s)}\]

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.059}{n} \log \frac{[\text{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\text{Cu}^{2+}]}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Evaluate the concentration ratio: \[\frac{[\text{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\text{Cu}^{2+}]} = \frac{0.1}{1.0} = 10^{-1}\] Compute the logarithmic term: \[\log(10^{-1}) = -1\] Substitute into the formula: \[E_{\text{cell}} = 1.10\text{ V} - \frac{0.059}{2}(-1) = 1.10\text{ V} + 0.0295\text{ V} = 1.1295\text{ V} \approx 1.13\text{ V}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Because reactant concentration exceeds product concentration, \(E_{\text{cell}} > E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\), yielding \(1.13\text{ V}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(1.13\text{ V}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q06 - Hydrogen electrode potential computation at specified solution acidity

questiontext.text: Calculate the potential of a hydrogen electrode at \(298\text{ K}\) dipping in an aqueous solution of \(\text{pH} = 4\) under a hydrogen gas pressure of \(1\text{ bar}\). (Take \(\frac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(\text{pH} = 4\).
Gas pressure: \(p_{\text{H}_2} = 1\text{ bar}\).
Temperature: \(T = 298\text{ K}\).
Electrode reaction: \(\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq}) + \mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\text{H}_2(\text{g})\).
Standard potential: \(E^\circ_{\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_2} = 0.00\text{ V}\).
Number of electrons: \(n = 1\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
From the definition of pH, \([\text{H}^{+}] = 10^{-\text{pH}} = 10^{-4}\text{ M}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[E_{\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_2} = E^\circ_{\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_2} - \frac{0.059}{1} \log \frac{1}{[\text{H}^{+}]} = -0.059 \times \text{pH}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[E_{\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_2} = -0.059 \times 4 = -0.236\text{ V}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
At \([\text{H}^{+}] = 10^{-4}\text{ M}\) (lower than standard \(1\text{ M}\)), the reduction potential is negative, equal to \(-0.236\text{ V}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(-0.236\text{ V}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q07 - Standard Gibbs free energy evaluation for zinc copper cell

questiontext.text: For the galvanic cell reaction \(\text{Zn(s)} + \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(\text{aq)} + \text{Cu(s)}\), the standard cell potential is \(1.10\text{ V}\). What is the standard Gibbs energy change (\(\Delta_r G^\circ\)) of this reaction? (Take \(F = 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Standard cell potential: \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 1.10\text{ V}\).
Moles of electrons transferred: \(n = 2\).
Faraday constant: \(F = 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
The standard Gibbs energy change is related to the standard cell electromotive force by the thermodynamic relation for reversible electrochemical work.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[\Delta_r G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{\text{cell}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\Delta_r G^\circ = -2 \times 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1} \times 1.10\text{ V} = -212271.4\text{ J mol}^{-1} \approx -212.27\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
A spontaneous reaction with positive \(E^\circ\) corresponds to a negative standard Gibbs energy of \(-212.27\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(-212.27\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q08 - Equilibrium constant computation for copper silver displacement reaction

questiontext.text:
The standard potential of the cell corresponding to the reaction:

\[\text{Cu(s)} + 2\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq)} + 2\text{Ag(s)}\]

is \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.46\text{ V}\) at \(298\text{ K}\). What is the equilibrium constant (\(K_c\)) of this reaction? (Take \(\frac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Reaction: \(\text{Cu(s)} + 2\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) \rightleftharpoons \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq)} + 2\text{Ag(s)}\).
Standard cell potential: \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.46\text{ V}\).
Number of electrons: \(n = 2\).
Factor: \(\frac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}\) at \(298\text{ K}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
At dynamic equilibrium, the cell potential drops to zero (\(E_{\text{cell}} = 0\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = \frac{0.059}{n} \log K_c \implies \log K_c = \frac{n E^\circ_{\text{cell}}}{0.059}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\log K_c = \frac{2 \times 0.46\text{ V}}{0.059\text{ V}} = \frac{0.92}{0.059} \approx 15.6\] Taking antilogarithm: \[K_c = 10^{15.6} = 10^{0.6} \times 10^{15} \approx 3.92 \times 10^{15}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
A standard potential of \(+0.46\text{ V}\) indicates an equilibrium constant of approximately \(3.92 \times 10^{15}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(3.92 \times 10^{15}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q09 - Resistivity and conductivity determination for cylindrical solution column

questiontext.text: A cylindrical column of an electrolytic solution has a diameter of \(1.0\text{ cm}\) and a length of \(50\text{ cm}\). Its electrical resistance is measured to be \(5.55 \times 10^3\ \Omega\). What are the resistivity (\(\rho\)) and conductivity (\(\kappa\)) of the solution in \(\text{cm}\)-based units?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Diameter: \(d = 1.0\text{ cm} \implies \text{radius } r = 0.5\text{ cm}\).
Length: \(l = 50\text{ cm}\).
Resistance: \(R = 5.55 \times 10^3\ \Omega\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
The column has uniform circular cross section. Cross-sectional area is \(A = \pi r^2\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[A = 3.14 \times (0.5\text{ cm})^2 = 0.785\text{ cm}^2\] \[\rho = \frac{R A}{l}\] \[\kappa = \frac{1}{\rho}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate resistivity: \[\rho = \frac{5.55 \times 10^3\ \Omega \times 0.785\text{ cm}^2}{50\text{ cm}} = 87.135\ \Omega\text{ cm}\] Calculate conductivity: \[\kappa = \frac{1}{87.135\ \Omega\text{ cm}} \approx 0.01148\text{ S cm}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Resistivity is \(87.14\ \Omega\text{ cm}\) and conductivity is \(0.01148\text{ S cm}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(\rho = 87.14\ \Omega\text{ cm}\) and \(\kappa = 0.01148\text{ S cm}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q10 - Limiting molar conductivity calculation of calcium chloride salt

questiontext.text:
Given the limiting molar ionic conductivities at \(298\text{ K}\):

\[\lambda^\circ(\text{Ca}^{2+}) = 119.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

\[\lambda^\circ(\text{Cl}^-) = 76.3\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

What is the limiting molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_m^\circ\)) of calcium chloride (\(\text{CaCl}_2\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(\lambda^\circ(\text{Ca}^{2+}) = 119.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).
\(\lambda^\circ(\text{Cl}^-) = 76.3\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Principles and Stoichiometry
\(\text{CaCl}_2\) dissociates completely at infinite dilution according to: \[\text{CaCl}_2 \rightarrow \text{Ca}^{2+} + 2\text{Cl}^-\] Stoichiometric coefficients are \(\nu_+ = 1\) and \(\nu_- = 2\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
By Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions: \[\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CaCl}_2) = \nu_+ \lambda^\circ(\text{Ca}^{2+}) + \nu_- \lambda^\circ(\text{Cl}^-) = \lambda^\circ(\text{Ca}^{2+}) + 2\lambda^\circ(\text{Cl}^-)\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CaCl}_2) = 119.0 + 2(76.3) = 119.0 + 152.6 = 271.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Sum of individual ion conductivities gives \(271.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(271.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q11 - Limiting molar conductivity determination for weak acetic acid

questiontext.text: The limiting molar conductivities (\(\Lambda_m^\circ\)) for \(\text{NaCl}\), \(\text{HCl}\), and \(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}\) at \(298\text{ K}\) are \(126.4\), \(425.9\), and \(91.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\), respectively. What is the value of \(\Lambda_m^\circ\) for acetic acid (\(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{HCl}) = 425.9\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).
\(\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}) = 91.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).
\(\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{NaCl}) = 126.4\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Principles and Algebraic Combination
By Kohlrausch's law: \[\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}) = \lambda^\circ(\text{H}^+) + \lambda^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-)\] This can be expressed as: \[\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}) = \Lambda_m^\circ(\text{HCl}) + \Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}) - \Lambda_m^\circ(\text{NaCl})\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
\[\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}) = 425.9 + 91.0 - 126.4 = 516.9 - 126.4 = 390.5\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The limiting molar conductivity of acetic acid is \(390.5\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(390.5\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q12 - Electricity required in Faradays for aluminium metal production

questiontext.text: How much electricity in terms of Faraday (\(F\)) is required to produce \(40.0\text{ g}\) of aluminium metal from molten \(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\)? (Molar mass of \(\text{Al} = 27.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of aluminium: \(m = 40.0\text{ g}\).
Molar mass of aluminium: \(M = 27.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).
Electrode reaction: \(\text{Al}^{3+} + 3\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Al(s)}\).

Step 2: Principles and Stoichiometry
Deposition of \(1\text{ mol}\) (\(27.0\text{ g}\)) of aluminium requires \(3\text{ moles}\) of electrons, which equals \(3\text{ F}\) of electricity.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[n_{\text{Al}} = \frac{m}{M}\] \[Q (\text{in } F) = n_{\text{Al}} \times 3\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[n_{\text{Al}} = \frac{40.0\text{ g}}{27.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}} \approx 1.4815\text{ mol}\] \[Q = 1.4815 \times 3\text{ F} \approx 4.44\text{ F}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The electricity required is \(4.44\text{ F}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(4.44\text{ F}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q13 - Number of electrons flowing through wire during electrolysis

questiontext.text: If a steady electric current of \(0.5\text{ A}\) flows through a metallic wire for \(2\text{ hours}\), how many electrons flow through the wire? (Take charge on an electron as \(1.602 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Current: \(I = 0.5\text{ A}\).
Time: \(t = 2\text{ hours} = 2 \times 3600\text{ s} = 7200\text{ s}\).
Elementary charge: \(e = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
Electric charge is the product of current and time: \(Q = I \times t\). Total number of electrons is \(N = Q / e\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[Q = I t\] \[N = \frac{Q}{e}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate total charge: \[Q = 0.5\text{ A} \times 7200\text{ s} = 3600\text{ C}\] Calculate number of electrons: \[N = \frac{3600\text{ C}}{1.602 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}} \approx 2.247 \times 10^{22} \approx 2.25 \times 10^{22}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
A charge of \(3600\text{ C}\) corresponds to \(2.25 \times 10^{22}\) electrons.

Final Conceptual Answer: \(2.25 \times 10^{22}\) electrons

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q14 - Quantity of electricity in coulombs for dichromate reduction

questiontext.text:
Consider the acidic reduction reaction of dichromate ion:

\[\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}(\text{aq}) + 14\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq}) + 6\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+}(\text{aq}) + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\]

What is the quantity of electricity in coulombs needed to reduce \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}\)? (Take \(F = 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Reaction: \(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^{+} + 6\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}\).
Amount of \(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}\): \(1\text{ mol}\).
Faraday constant: \(F = 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Principles and Stoichiometry
From the balanced half-reaction, reduction of \(1\text{ mol}\) of dichromate requires \(6\text{ moles}\) of electrons (\(6\text{ F}\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[Q = n \times F = 6 \times F\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[Q = 6 \times 96487\text{ C} = 578922\text{ C} \approx 5.79 \times 10^5\text{ C}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The quantity of electricity is \(5.79 \times 10^5\text{ C}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(5.79 \times 10^5\text{ C}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q15 - Nernst equation cell potential calculation for magnesium silver system

questiontext.text:
A galvanic cell operates according to the reaction:

\[\text{Mg(s)} + 2\text{Ag}^{+}(0.0001\text{ M}) \rightarrow \text{Mg}^{2+}(0.130\text{ M}) + 2\text{Ag(s)}\]

Given that \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 3.17\text{ V}\) and \(\frac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}\) at \(298\text{ K}\), what is the cell electromotive force (\(E_{\text{cell}}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Standard cell potential: \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 3.17\text{ V}\).
Concentrations: \([\text{Mg}^{2+}] = 0.130\text{ M}\), \([\text{Ag}^{+}] = 0.0001\text{ M} = 10^{-4}\text{ M}\).
Moles of electrons: \(n = 2\).
Factor: \(\frac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}\) at \(298\text{ K}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
Solid magnesium and solid silver have constant unit activities.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.059}{n} \log \frac{[\text{Mg}^{2+}]}{[\text{Ag}^{+}]^2}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate reaction quotient: \[Q = \frac{0.130}{(10^{-4})^2} = \frac{0.130}{10^{-8}} = 1.30 \times 10^7\] Evaluate logarithm: \[\log(1.30 \times 10^7) = \log 1.30 + 7 \approx 0.1139 + 7 = 7.1139\] Compute reduction term: \[\frac{0.059}{2} \times 7.1139 \approx 0.0295 \times 7.1139 \approx 0.21\text{ V}\] Calculate cell potential: \[E_{\text{cell}} = 3.17\text{ V} - 0.21\text{ V} = 2.96\text{ V}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The cell potential is \(2.96\text{ V}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(2.96\text{ V}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q16 - Nernst equation potential calculation for tin hydrogen gas cell

questiontext.text:
For the electrochemical cell at \(298\text{ K}\):

\[\text{Sn(s)} \mid \text{Sn}^{2+}(0.050\text{ M}) \parallel \text{H}^{+}(0.020\text{ M}) \mid \text{H}_2(\text{g}, 1\text{ bar}) \mid \text{Pt(s)}\]

Given standard potentials \(E^\circ_{\text{Sn}^{2+}/\text{Sn}} = -0.14\text{ V}\), \(E^\circ_{\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_2} = 0.00\text{ V}\), and \(\frac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}\), what is the cell potential (\(E_{\text{cell}}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Anode reaction: \(\text{Sn(s)} \rightarrow \text{Sn}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^-\), \(E^\circ = -0.14\text{ V}\).
Cathode reaction: \(2\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2(\text{g})\), \(E^\circ = 0.00\text{ V}\).
Overall reaction: \(\text{Sn(s)} + 2\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Sn}^{2+}(\text{aq)} + \text{H}_2(\text{g})\).
Number of electrons: \(n = 2\).
Concentrations: \([\text{Sn}^{2+}] = 0.050\text{ M}\), \([\text{H}^{+}] = 0.020\text{ M}\), \(p_{\text{H}_2} = 1\text{ bar}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
\[E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}} = 0.00 - (-0.14) = +0.14\text{ V}\]

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.059}{2} \log \frac{[\text{Sn}^{2+}] p_{\text{H}_2}}{[\text{H}^{+}]^2}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Compute reaction quotient: \[Q = \frac{0.050 \times 1}{(0.020)^2} = \frac{0.050}{0.00040} = 125\] Compute logarithm: \[\log 125 = \log(5^3) = 3 \log 5 = 3 \times 0.69897 = 2.0969\] Compute deduction term: \[\frac{0.059}{2} \times 2.0969 = 0.0295 \times 2.0969 \approx 0.0619\text{ V} \approx 0.062\text{ V}\] Calculate cell potential: \[E_{\text{cell}} = 0.14\text{ V} - 0.062\text{ V} = 0.078\text{ V}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The cell potential is \(0.078\text{ V}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(0.078\text{ V}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q17 - Standard Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant for ferric iodide system

questiontext.text:
For the cell in which the reaction occurs at \(298\text{ K}\):

\[2\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq}) + 2\text{I}^{-}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+}(\text{aq)} + \text{I}_2(\text{s})\]

The standard cell potential is \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.236\text{ V}\). Taking \(F = 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\) and \(\frac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}\), what are the standard Gibbs energy change (\(\Delta_r G^\circ\)) and the equilibrium constant (\(K_c\)) of the reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Reaction: \(2\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq}) + 2\text{I}^{-}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+}(\text{aq)} + \text{I}_2(\text{s})\).
Standard cell potential: \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.236\text{ V}\).
Moles of electrons: \(n = 2\).
Faraday constant: \(F = 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae
\[\Delta_r G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{\text{cell}}\] \[\log K_c = \frac{n E^\circ_{\text{cell}}}{0.059}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate \(\Delta_r G^\circ\): \[\Delta_r G^\circ = -2 \times 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1} \times 0.236\text{ V} = -45541.86\text{ J mol}^{-1} \approx -45.54\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\] Calculate \(\log K_c\): \[\log K_c = \frac{2 \times 0.236}{0.059} = \frac{0.472}{0.059} = 8.0\] Taking antilogarithm: \[K_c = 10^{8.0} \text{ (or } 9.62 \times 10^7 \text{ using exact } 0.05916\text{ V)}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
\(\Delta_r G^\circ = -45.54\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) and \(K_c = 9.62 \times 10^7\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(\Delta_r G^\circ = -45.54\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) and \(K_c = 9.62 \times 10^7\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q18 - Degree of dissociation and dissociation constant for methanoic acid

questiontext.text: The molar conductivity of \(0.025\text{ mol L}^{-1}\) methanoic acid (\(\text{HCOOH}\)) is \(46.1\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\). Given limiting ionic conductivities \(\lambda^\circ(\text{H}^+) = 349.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\) and \(\lambda^\circ(\text{HCOO}^-) = 54.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\), what are its degree of dissociation (\(\alpha\)) and dissociation constant (\(K_a\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Concentration: \(c = 0.025\text{ mol L}^{-1}\).
Molar conductivity: \(\Lambda_m = 46.1\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).
Limiting conductivities: \(\lambda^\circ(\text{H}^+) = 349.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\), \(\lambda^\circ(\text{HCOO}^-) = 54.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae
\[\Lambda_m^\circ = \lambda^\circ(\text{H}^+) + \lambda^\circ(\text{HCOO}^-)\] \[\alpha = \frac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^\circ}\] \[K_a = \frac{c \alpha^2}{1 - \alpha}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate limiting molar conductivity: \[\Lambda_m^\circ = 349.6 + 54.6 = 404.2\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\] Calculate degree of dissociation: \[\alpha = \frac{46.1}{404.2} \approx 0.11405 \approx 0.114\] Calculate dissociation constant: \[K_a = \frac{0.025 \times (0.114)^2}{1 - 0.114} = \frac{0.025 \times 0.012996}{0.886} \approx 3.67 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mol L}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
\(\alpha = 0.114\) and \(K_a = 3.67 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mol L}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(\alpha = 0.114\) and \(K_a = 3.67 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mol L}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q19 - Sequential cell constant conductivity and molar conductivity computation

questiontext.text: The resistance of a conductivity cell filled with \(0.1\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ KCl}\) solution is \(100\ \Omega\). When the same cell is filled with \(0.02\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ KCl}\) solution, the resistance is \(520\ \Omega\). Given that the conductivity of \(0.1\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ KCl}\) solution is \(1.29\text{ S m}^{-1}\), what are the conductivity (\(\kappa\)) and molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_m\)) of the \(0.02\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ KCl}\) solution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
First solution (\(0.1\text{ M KCl}\)): \(R_1 = 100\ \Omega\), \(\kappa_1 = 1.29\text{ S m}^{-1}\).
Second solution (\(0.02\text{ M KCl}\)): \(R_2 = 520\ \Omega\), \(c_2 = 0.02\text{ mol L}^{-1} = 20\text{ mol m}^{-3}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae
\[G^* = R_1 \times \kappa_1\] \[\kappa_2 = \frac{G^*}{R_2}\] \[\Lambda_m = \frac{\kappa_2}{c_2}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate cell constant: \[G^* = 100\ \Omega \times 1.29\text{ S m}^{-1} = 129\text{ m}^{-1} = 1.29\text{ cm}^{-1}\] Calculate conductivity of \(0.02\text{ M KCl}\): \[\kappa_2 = \frac{129\text{ m}^{-1}}{520\ \Omega} \approx 0.248\text{ S m}^{-1} = 0.248 \times 10^{-2}\text{ S cm}^{-1}\] Calculate molar conductivity: \[\Lambda_m = \frac{0.248\text{ S m}^{-1}}{20\text{ mol m}^{-3}} = 124 \times 10^{-4}\text{ S m}^2\text{ mol}^{-1} = 124\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
\(\kappa = 0.248\text{ S m}^{-1}\) and \(\Lambda_m = 124\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(\kappa = 0.248\text{ S m}^{-1}\) and \(\Lambda_m = 124\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q20 - Series electrolytic cells analysis using Faraday laws of electrolysis

questiontext.text: Three electrolytic cells A, B, and C containing solutions of \(\text{ZnSO}_4\), \(\text{AgNO}_3\), and \(\text{CuSO}_4\) respectively are connected in series. A steady current of \(1.5\text{ A}\) is passed through them until \(1.45\text{ g}\) of silver is deposited at the cathode of cell B. How long did the current flow, and what masses of copper and zinc were deposited? (Take atomic masses: \(\text{Ag} = 108.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), \(\text{Cu} = 63.5\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), \(\text{Zn} = 65.4\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), and \(F = 96500\text{ C mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of silver: \(m_{\text{Ag}} = 1.45\text{ g}\).
Current: \(I = 1.5\text{ A}\).
Molar masses: \(\text{Ag} = 108.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), \(\text{Cu} = 63.5\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), \(\text{Zn} = 65.4\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).
Faraday constant: \(F = 96500\text{ C mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
Cells are connected in series, meaning the exact same quantity of electricity \(Q\) passes through all three cells.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
Charge passed: \[Q = \frac{m_{\text{Ag}}}{108.0} \times 96500\] Time: \[t = \frac{Q}{I}\] By Faraday's second law: \[\frac{m_{\text{Cu}}}{\text{Eq. wt of Cu}} = \frac{m_{\text{Zn}}}{\text{Eq. wt of Zn}} = \frac{m_{\text{Ag}}}{\text{Eq. wt of Ag}}\] where \(\text{Eq. wt of Ag} = 108.0\), \(\text{Eq. wt of Cu} = \frac{63.5}{2} = 31.75\), \(\text{Eq. wt of Zn} = \frac{65.4}{2} = 32.7\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Charge: \[Q = \frac{1.45}{108.0} \times 96500 \approx 1295.6\text{ C}\] Time: \[t = \frac{1295.6\text{ C}}{1.5\text{ A}} \approx 863.7\text{ s} \approx 14.4\text{ minutes}\] Mass of copper deposited: \[m_{\text{Cu}} = 1.45 \times \frac{31.75}{108.0} \approx 0.426\text{ g}\] Mass of zinc deposited: \[m_{\text{Zn}} = 1.45 \times \frac{32.7}{108.0} \approx 0.439\text{ g}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Current flowed for \(14.4\text{ min}\); \(0.426\text{ g}\) of copper and \(0.439\text{ g}\) of zinc were deposited.

Final Conceptual Answer: \(t = 14.4\text{ min}\), \(m_{\text{Cu}} = 0.426\text{ g}\), and \(m_{\text{Zn}} = 0.439\text{ g}\)
